title: India Overtakes Russia as Fourth-Largest Forex Reserve Holder After Record $44.9B Surge
excerpt: The RBI said reserves jumped a record $44.9 billion to a lifetime high of $785.7 billion in the week ended September 4, driven by the central bank's FCNR(B) deposit scheme — with a Rs 1 lakh crore bond sale now planned to mop up excess liquidity.
body:
• India's foreign exchange reserves rose a record $44.903 billion to a lifetime high of $785.706 billion in the week ended September 4, 2026 — the largest single-week increase on record, according to Reserve Bank of India data released Friday.
  • The jump lifted India past Russia to become the world's fourth-largest forex reserve holder, behind only China, Japan and Switzerland, Bloomberg data showed.
  • Foreign currency assets climbed $47.498 billion to $648.168 billion, more than offsetting a $2.594 billion decline in gold reserves to $113.816 billion as gold prices fell.
  • The inflows were driven by the RBI's concessional FCNR(B) deposit scheme, launched June 8, which drew in more than $136 billion before the central bank closed the window on August 31, ahead of its September 30 expiry.
  • To mop up the resulting excess liquidity, the RBI announced a Rs 1 lakh crore open market sale of government bonds in three tranches across September.

India's foreign exchange reserves jumped by a record $44.903 billion to a lifetime high of $785.706 billion in the week ended September 4, the Reserve Bank of India said on Friday, in a surge that has made India the world's fourth-largest forex reserve holder. The increase, the largest single-week rise on record, displaced Russia from the fourth spot, leaving India behind only China, Japan and Switzerland, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The scale of the jump is exceptional even by the standards of a reserves series that has climbed steadily through the year. In the previous reporting week, the kitty had risen $11.475 billion to a then-all-time high of $740.803 billion. The latest week's near-$45 billion addition is almost four times that.

What drove the record inflow

The surge was powered by the RBI's foreign currency non-resident (bank) — or FCNR(B) — deposit scheme, a concessional forex swap initiative launched on June 8 to attract dollar inflows as the rupee came under pressure. The window was originally scheduled to stay open until September 30, but the central bank closed it on August 31, saying the program had achieved its objective ahead of schedule. By then it had yielded more than $136 billion in new flows, with banks mobilizing $127.226 billion through the scheme and overseas foreign-currency borrowings and external commercial borrowings adding to the total.

Foreign currency assets, the largest component of the reserves, rose $47.498 billion to $648.168 billion during the week. Expressed in dollar terms, that component also reflects the appreciation or depreciation of non-U.S. currencies such as the euro, pound and yen held in the reserves. The rise in foreign currency assets more than offset a $2.594 billion decline in the value of the RBI's gold holdings to $113.816 billion, following a fall in gold prices. Special drawing rights were down $4 million at $18.806 billion, while India's reserve position with the IMF rose $2 million to $4.916 billion.

Rebound after West Asia pressure

The record inflow caps a sharp reversal. India's reserves had been declining since the start of the conflict in West Asia earlier this year, as the rupee came under pressure and the RBI sold dollars to curb volatility. Total reserves had fallen to $666.9 billion in the week ended June 26 before the FCNR(B) window turned the tide. A larger forex kitty gives the RBI more headroom to intervene in spot and forward currency markets and keep the rupee's movement orderly during periods of stress.

Mopping up the liquidity flood

The strong inflows have created a problem of plenty: substantial excess liquidity in the domestic banking system. In response, the RBI has moved aggressively to absorb surplus cash. The central bank announced an open market operation sale of government bonds worth Rs 1 lakh crore, to be conducted in three tranches — Rs 50,000 crore on September 17, Rs 25,000 crore on September 21 and another Rs 25,000 crore on September 28 — through the multiple-price method using a multi-security auction.

Earlier in the week, the RBI had already raised more than Rs 3.53 lakh crore through an overnight Variable Rate Reverse Repo auction with a one-day tenor to drain surplus cash from the banking system.

What it signals

An increase in foreign exchange reserves reflects strong economic fundamentals and hands the central bank a deeper buffer against external shocks — energy-price volatility, capital-flow reversals, or renewed geopolitical turbulence in West Asia. With $785.7 billion in reserves and a demonstrated ability to draw large inflows on demand, the RBI enters the year's final quarter with its firepower at an all-time high. The next test comes with the bond sale tranches, which will show how cleanly the banking system absorbs the withdrawal of Rs 1 lakh crore without disrupting yields.
image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India building in Mumbai. Forex reserves rose a record $44.9 billion to $785.7 billion, lifting India past Russia to become the world's fourth-largest holder.
nri_angle: A record forex stockpile strengthens the rupee's floor against global shocks, which directly affects exchange rates for remittances and the returns of India-linked portfolios.
